steps.name: prompt
steps.text: Write the introduction for our paper comparing centralized, decentralized and hybrid LLM dialogue frameworks for multi-robot task planning, with a focus on how they scale to many robots.

steps.name: skeleton_outline
steps.text:
- Multi-robot systems: promise and planning challenges; limits of prior methods
- LLMs as task planners: single-agent success, early multi-robot work
- Scaling problems of one-LLM-per-robot
- Our goal and the four frameworks compared
- Novelty and main findings

steps.name: detailed_outline
steps.text:
- Multi-robot systems
  - great potential for many-task operations, e.g. warehouse management
  - planning hard: heterogeneous capabilities, coordination on multi-robot tasks, task inter-dependencies, safety (collision avoidance)
  - difficulty scales with number of robots
  - previous: algorithm-based (cite) or learning-based (cite)
  - tuned to specific scenario, heavy engineering, poor generalization to novel tasks/scenarios
- LLMs as planners
  - pre-trained LLMs generalize to new task domains (cite)
  - many recent efforts for single-agent task planning (cite)
  - better planning via context: initial prompts (in-context learning, chain-of-thought) or iterative re-prompting with feedback (environment state changes, detected errors)
  - new interest: LLMs as multi-robot task planners (cite)
  - two or three robots; one LLM per robot; collaborative dialogue rounds
- Scaling issues (one LLM agent per robot)
  - coordinating actions and inter-dependencies grow exponentially with agents -> harder reasoning
  - context: other LLMs' responses this round + history of dialogue, actions, states -> token length toward modern limits, longer inference runtime (and API costs)
  - relevant info diluted in longer prompts
  - beyond scope of prior work (cite)
- Our goal / approach
  - keep LLM generalizability, address scaling to many agents
  - argue framework choice improves scalability and success rates
  - compare four frameworks (Figure 3), increasing robot numbers; incremental planning, next action per agent
  - DMAS: decentralized, LLM per robot, turn-taking rounds
  - CMAS: centralized, single LLM gives next action for all robots
  - hybrids: HMAS-1 (DMAS + central LLM initial plan to prime dialogue); CMAS + per-robot LLMs giving robot-local feedback to central planner
  - truncated prompt: only state-action info from prior rounds (token length)
  - evaluation: four warehouse-inspired task planning environments; simulated 3D manipulation task needing coordination among manipulators
- Novelty / findings
  - first study of scalability of LLM dialogue frameworks for multi-robot planning
  - HMAS-2 + state-action history greatly improve success rates with many robots

steps.name: partial_draft
steps.text:
Multi-robot systems have a lot of potential as a tool for operations where many tasks have to be completed, for example warehouse management. Planning for these systems is often hard because of heterogeneous robot capabilities, coordination during tasks that need multiple robots, inter-dependencies between separate tasks, and general safety considerations (e.g. collision avoidance). The difficulty also scales with the number of robots. Previous work has used algorithm-based or learning-based methods to control multi-robot systems. These approaches are usually tuned for a specific scenario, and they need a lot of engineering effort, which limits how well they generalize to novel tasks or scenarios.

Pre-trained large language models (LLMs) are able to generalize to new task domains, and this has motivated many recent efforts to use them for single-agent task planning. Planning performance gets much better when the context given to the LLM is used cleverly, either with techniques for the initial prompts (e.g., in-context learning, chain-of-thought) or with iterative re-prompting with feedback (e.g., environment state changes, detected errors). Because of this success there is new interest in using LLMs as task planners for multi-robot systems. These recent efforts look at systems with two or three robots. They assign an LLM to each robot and the models have collaborative dialogue rounds to try to find good plans.

- Scaling issues for one-LLM-per-robot:
  - possible coordinating actions + inter-dependencies grow exponentially with agents -> harder reasoning
  - context includes all other LLMs' responses this round + history of dialogue/actions/states -> token length toward modern limits, more inference runtime and API costs
  - relevant info diluted in long prompts; beyond scope of prior work
- Our goal: keep generalizability, address scaling; frameworks matter for scalability and success rates
  - four frameworks (Figure 3), incremental planning of next action per agent
  - DMAS (decentralized, turn-taking), CMAS (single central LLM), HMAS-1 (DMAS + central initial plan), CMAS variant with robot-local feedback LLMs
  - truncated prompt with only state-action info from prior rounds
  - four warehouse-inspired environments + simulated 3D manipulation task
- First study of scalability of LLM dialogue frameworks for multi-robot planning; HMAS-2 + state-action history greatly improve success with many robots

steps.name: rough_draft
steps.text:
Multi-robot systems have a lot of potential as a tool for operations where many tasks have to be completed, for example warehouse management. Planning for these systems is often hard because of heterogeneous robot capabilities, coordination during tasks that need multiple robots, inter-dependencies between separate tasks, and general safety considerations (e.g. collision avoidance). The difficulty also scales with the number of robots. Previous work has used algorithm-based or learning-based methods to control multi-robot systems. These approaches are usually tuned for a specific scenario, and they need a lot of engineering effort, which limits how well they generalize to novel tasks or scenarios.

Pre-trained large language models (LLMs) are able to generalize to new task domains, and this has motivated many recent efforts to use them for single-agent task planning. Planning performance gets much better when the context given to the LLM is used cleverly, either with techniques for the initial prompts (e.g., in-context learning, chain-of-thought) or with iterative re-prompting with feedback (e.g., environment state changes, detected errors). Because of this success there is new interest in using LLMs as task planners for multi-robot systems. These recent efforts look at systems with two or three robots. They assign an LLM to each robot and the models have collaborative dialogue rounds to try to find good plans.

Approaches that assign each robot its own LLM agent have a problem when scaling to systems with many robots and tasks with longer horizons. First, the number of possible coordinating actions and the possible action inter-dependencies both grow exponentially with the number of agents, and this makes reasoning harder for the language models. Second, the context that each LLM gets contains the responses of every other LLM for the current round of dialogue, plus the history of dialogue, actions, and states from earlier rounds. So scaling the number of agents also scales the context token length requirements toward their modern limits, and it increases the runtime of LLM inference (and API costs). Also, the information that is immediately relevant in the context can get diluted in longer prompts. These limitations are beyond the scope of prior work.

Our goal is to keep the generalizability of LLMs as task planners for multi-robot settings, while dealing with the challenges of scaling to many agents. We argue that different frameworks for integrating LLM planners into multi-robot task planning can improve scalability and also task planning success rates. In this work we compare four different frameworks (Figure 3) of cooperative dialogue for task planning among multiple LLMs, for increasing numbers of robots. In each one, planning is done incrementally, and the LLMs collaborate to find the next action to take for each agent in the system. The first approach (DMAS) uses a decentralized communication framework where each robot gets its own LLM agent and the dialogue goes in rounds of turn-taking. The second approach (CMAS) uses a centralized framework where one single LLM produces the next action for all robots in the system. We also propose two hybrid versions of these approaches: (1) a variant of DMAS that adds a central LLM that is responsible for giving an initial plan to prime the dialogue (HMAS-1) and (2) a variant of CMAS that gives each robot an LLM which provides robot-local feedback to the central LLM planner. To further deal with the token length issues from historical dialogue and planning context, we also propose a truncated prompt that only includes state-action information from prior dialogue rounds. We evaluate how each approach performs in four different task planning environments inspired by warehouse settings. To further demonstrate LLMs as multi-robot planners, we also apply these approaches to a simulated 3D manipulation task that needs coordination among the manipulators.

As far as we know, this work is the first to study the scalability of different LLM dialogue frameworks for multi-robot planning. The proposed HMAS-2 framework and the state-action history method improve the planning success rates a lot when there are many robots.

steps.name: revised_draft
steps.text:
Multi-robot systems have great potential as a tool for operations that require the completion of many tasks, such as warehouse management. Planning for these systems is often challenging due to heterogeneous robot capabilities, coordination during tasks requiring multiple robots, inter-dependencies of separate tasks, and general safety considerations (e.g. collision avoidance). Moreover, the difficulty scales with the number of robots. Previous work has used algorithm-based [1,2,3] or learning-based [4,5] methods to control multi-robot systems. Such approaches are typically tuned for a specific scenario and require significant engineering effort, which limits generalization to novel tasks or scenarios.

Motivated by the ability of pre-trained large language models (LLMs) to generalize to new task domains [6,7], there have been many recent efforts to use them for single-agent task planning [8,9]. Planning performance is significantly improved through clever use of the context provided to the LLM, whether via techniques for initial prompts (e.g., in-context learning, chain-of-thought) or iterative re-prompting with feedback (e.g., environment state changes, detected errors). Given this success, there is new interest in investigating LLMs as task planners for multi-robot systems [10,11]. These recent efforts address systems of two or three robots; they assign an LLM to each robot and have the models engage in collaborative dialogue rounds to find good plans.

Scaling to systems of many robots and tasks with longer horizons is an issue for approaches that assign each robot its own LLM agent. First, both the number of possible coordinating actions and the possible action inter-dependencies grow exponentially with the number of agents, making reasoning more difficult for the language models. Second, the context provided to each LLM contains the responses of every other LLM for the current round of dialogue in addition to the history of dialogue, actions, and states from prior rounds; scaling the number of agents therefore also scales the context token length requirements toward their modern limits and increases the runtime of LLM inference (and API costs). In addition, the immediately relevant information in the context can become diluted in longer prompts. These limitations are beyond the scope of prior work [10,11].

Our goal is to preserve the generalizability of LLMs as task planners for multi-robot settings while addressing the challenges of scaling to many agents. We argue that different frameworks for integrating LLM planners into multi-robot task planning can improve both scalability and task planning success rates. In this work, we compare four different frameworks (Figure 3) of cooperative dialogue for task planning among multiple LLMs for increasing numbers of robots. In each, planning is performed incrementally, with the LLMs collaborating to find the next action for each agent in the system. The first approach (DMAS) uses a decentralized communication framework in which each robot is given its own LLM agent and dialogue proceeds in rounds of turn-taking. The second approach (CMAS) uses a centralized framework in which a single LLM produces the next action for all robots in the system. We also propose two hybrid versions of these approaches: (1) a variant of DMAS that adds a central LLM responsible for providing an initial plan to prime the dialogue (HMAS-1) and (2) a variant of CMAS that gives each robot an LLM to provide robot-local feedback to the central LLM planner. To further address token length issues due to historical dialogue and planning context, we also propose a truncated prompt that includes only state-action information from prior dialogue rounds. We evaluate the performance of each approach in four different task planning environments inspired by warehouse settings. To further demonstrate LLMs as multi-robot planners, we apply these approaches to a simulated 3D manipulation task requiring coordination among the manipulators.

To the best of our knowledge, this work is the first to study the scalability of different LLM dialogue frameworks for multi-robot planning. The proposed HMAS-2 framework and state-action history method greatly improve planning success rates in settings with high numbers of robots.
